analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal rulemaking to add cost-benefit, formal-hearing, and court hurdles before agencies can issue major regulations.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee approved the bill on Feb. 14, 2018, and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the Administrative Procedure Act, the basic rulebook for how federal agencies write regulations. For large rules (over $100 million in economic effects) and very large rules (over $1 billion), it requires agencies to pick the cheapest workable option, give companies a formal public hearing with cross-examination of the agency's evidence, run every draft past the White House regulatory office, and defend rules under a stricter court standard. Supporters called it regulatory transparency and accountability; the practical effect is that federal health, safety, financial, and environmental protections become slower to issue, easier to challenge in court, and weaker at the moment of adoption.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies regulated by federal agencies — energy producers, chemical manufacturers, automakers, drug makers, banks, and other large regulated firms — gain procedural tools to delay, dilute, or defeat major rules before they take effect, and corporate law firms gain a larger docket of hearings and court challenges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated industries and corporate law firms

how_it_helps.text: For rules projected to cost the economy $1 billion or more, and certain $100 million rules, interested companies can demand a formal public hearing with oral presentation, cross-examination of witnesses, and the burden of proof on the agency proposing the rule — turning rulemaking into a litigation-like forum only well-funded parties can fully use.

Agencies must adopt the most cost-effective rule among alternatives for major rules, and can only choose a more protective rule if they can specifically justify that its extra benefits outweigh its extra costs — a framework that disfavors protections whose benefits, like lives saved, are hard to price.

Agencies must notify the White House regulatory office (OIRA) before proposing rules, provide at least 90 days of comment for major rules, and publish detailed cost-benefit analyses, adding review layers and time to every major rulemaking.

The bill creates a new 'substantial evidence' court standard for $1 billion rules, lets courts send rules back to agencies without overturning them, and bars courts from reviewing how an agency classified a rule's cost effects — reshaping judicial review in ways that extend litigation over rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal rules for clean air and water, workplace safety, food and product safety, and fair treatment by banks and other companies, because protections arrive slower, face more challenges, and must clear a cost-first test; agencies also pay in staff time and slower action.

drawbacks.text: Formal hearings with cross-examination and new court standards let well-funded corporate litigants relitigate contested scientific and technical questions, drawing out rulemakings for years — a burden that opponents, including committee Democrats who filed formal minority views, argued would stall critical protections.

The requirement to adopt the most cost-effective rule can block stronger health and safety protections when benefits like avoided illness or death are real but hard to quantify, an honest cost even a supporter of cost-benefit discipline would acknowledge.

Supporters acknowledged the bill makes rulemaking slower and more expensive for agencies with limited staff, and the bill itself builds in exemptions — monetary policy is excluded, and agencies can bypass the new procedures under a 'good cause' finding — which undercuts the uniform accountability its sponsors advertised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers some genuine transparency — public dockets, longer comment periods, and a bar on agencies using federal money to lobby for their own proposed rules — but its headline mechanisms (mandatory cheapest-rule adoption, formal hearings with cross-examination, and harder court standards) operate as procedural choke points, not safeguards. Because only organizations with large legal budgets can effectively use hearings and litigation, the changes tilt the regulatory playing field toward regulated firms and away from the public the rules protect. On balance, the costs to timely, protective regulation outweigh the transparency gains.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the bill never came up for a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rob Portman (R-OH) introduced the bill on April 26, 2017, with bipartisan cosponsors, and it was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on May 17, 2017, and formally reported it on Feb. 14, 2018, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute; committee Democrats filed formal minority views.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 312), the list of business awaiting floor action, but the Senate never took it up for a vote before the 115th Congress ended on Jan. 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal agencies kept the existing rulemaking process, and current health, safety, and financial protections stayed intact; regulated industries gained nothing but also lost nothing, having preferred the bill's procedural changes. The main beneficiaries of the outcome were ordinary people who continue to rely on rules issued under the current process.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's nine cosponsors, seven were Republicans and two were Democrats (Sens. Heitkamp of North Dakota and Manchin of West Virginia), and the Republican-led committee advanced it over the objection of committee Democrats, who filed minority views.

industries.industry: Heavily regulated manufacturers and energy companies
industries.note: These firms would gain the right to demand formal hearings with cross-examination and would benefit from a mandate that agencies pick the cheapest adequate rule, delaying and weakening environmental, chemical, and workplace safety rules. The industry's gain comes directly at the cost of the protections ordinary people rely on.

Consumer financial rules issued by regulators would face the same comment periods, OIRA review, and cost-first adoption requirements, slowing rules like those governing fees and disclosure. The benefit to the industry is a slower, weaker rulebook.

Formal hearings, cross-examination, a new substantial-evidence court standard, and remand without vacatur create a larger market for regulatory litigation. Only parties able to afford extended proceedings — typically regulated firms — can fully use these tools.

Agencies would face mandatory dockets, timetables, cost-benefit frameworks, periodic retrospective assessments, and OIRA sign-off, consuming staff resources. Their interest in doing their statutory jobs aligns with the public's interest in timely protections.
